Deus Ex: Human Revolution is the prequel to my favorite game ever made: Deus Ex. Since I had already put the precursor to this title on a pedestal and was hyped to all hell, how does this game fare in comparison?

Not bad, actually.

Because this game is a prequel, it is totally fine to jump in and start playing it even without playing the previous games, although I caught many references and call backs to Deus Ex throughout. In fact, I’d probably recommend most players today to start with this game, as Deus Ex hasn’t really aged all that well in terms of graphics/ mechanics.

Deus Ex was a Cyberpunk dystopian FPS/RPG hybrid that was full of deep choices and free-form gameplay. The storyline dealt with world spanning conspiracies and epic world ending narratives, but Deus Ex: Human Revolution takes a smaller, more focused approach, mainly dealing with the basic morality question of human augmentation, corporate espionage, and how technology positively and/or negatively impacts the “natural” human experience. This smaller approach was somewhat disappointing at first as it’s not nearly as “epic” as the first game, but it still told an interesting story, full of little peeks at the larger conspiracies overall. The main character has the  pretty cliché motivation of revenge and delves into a complex web of intrigue that’ll keep you guessing until the very end. The ending is somewhat lackluster, but the upcoming sequel Mankind Divided promises more nuanced endings that depend on factors through the game. All in all, the many different character’s motivations and the many moral choices you make in the game paint a convincing near future cyberpunk world that is easy to get immersed in.

This game isn’t the prettiest, being initially released in 2011, but even back then it didn’t look so great. 2011 was the year Skyrim, Dead Space 2, L.A. Noire, Battlefield 3, and Arkham City were released. Deus Ex: Human Revolution already looked dated back then compare to these titles. However, the game remedies this with clear art direction. Most locations are flush with a calming and surreal old yellowed parchment art style that bathes the world in amber-yellow hues. The effect was designed to give the world a Renaissance style, with people learning so much about the human body and augmentation that extreme advancements were occurring rapidly, without the necessary societal changes to keep up. There is also plenty of Icarus/ Daedalus parallels as well, with humanity flying too close to the sun and getting burned as a result. Animations are mostly decent, but facial animations are pretty wooden and everyone looks somewhat like plastic. However, this game’s strikingly distinct art style more than makes up for the lackluster animations and textures and is one of the more memorable parts of the game.

The great part of this game’s design is it’s free-form approach to quests. You can complete the game without killing a single character (except the boss fights), and in some situations you can talk your way into areas that would normally be considered trespassing. For example, a quest near the beginning of the game requires you to retrieve something from a police station, which is off limits to civilians. However, you can either talk your way in (using CASIE augmentations if necessary), stealth your way in through a back alley, or kick in the front door and start shooting people in the face. Anytime a game allows me multiple approaches makes me feel like I’m actually using my own wits and not just blindly following a waypoint, although there are some quests that boil down to just that, unfortunately. Nevertheless, this level of freedom does a good job of reminding me why Deus Ex 1 was so good, as there were multiple approaches in that game as well. Going in guns blazing is viable, although the shooting mechanics feel a bit clunky compared to other FPSes.

This is also an RPG in addition to being an FPS, and there are different augmentations(skills) to put Praxis Points (Level ups) into. For example, if you’re making a loud, guns blazing character, you may want to invest in recoil management, Dermal Armor, and the Typhoon Explosive System, essentially an AOE attack that blows everything up in a 360 angle around you. However, if you’re a sneaky beaky kind of guy you may want to upgrade your ability to see enemy’s cones of vision on your minimap, as well as cloaking yourself. If you want to explore all the nooks and crannies the game has to offer you may want to upgrade your legs to jump super high and land from great heights without taking fall damage. There are many different things to level up, although I wished there were a bit more. It looks like Mankind Divided will have many more skills to try out, which I’m very excited for. One thing I felt was pretty OP was the cloaking in this game. Enemies can still hear you running around, but as long as you have plenty of cyberboost proenergy candy bars, you can make your way through most levels just by constantly gorging yourself on candy bars with cloak activated and running through the levels, awkwardly sidestepping enemies like Harry Potter with his invisibility cloak. Hopefully in Mankind Divided they nerf this, or at least make special enemies who can see through cloak or something.

Deus Ex: Human Revolution is a great Cyberpunk FPS/RPG that everyone who has an interest in the genre should play. It’s a prequel to one of the best games ever made in my opinion, and while it doesn’t quite live up to the first game, is still a fantastic experience in its own right. This game often goes on sale for $5, and at that price, it’s a no brainer considering you’ll get 20-25 hours of solid entertainment out of the experience. I’m very excited for Mankind Divided.

This isn't really Deus Ex.

I've dipped into this wayward IP several times since the original game captivated me, and I could never really grasp why none of these games felt quite as gripping as Deus Ex. It was difficult to pinpoint because Adam Jensen's story is absolutely substantial and well-written. The gameplay is certainly excellent in its own right, with a respectable balance between thorough stealth and open combat intensity. And the music also paints the world with an air fitting this dark and pragmatic environment. But I think I'm beginning to understand that these are not defining hallmarks of Deus Ex.

Watching through the Making Of video included in the extras of this game, I've found that they highlighted the exact departures that have guided this franchise to its grave for the second time. Deus Ex is meant to be total free reign play, guided by conspiracy theory and sci-fi fantasy, a world that is serious but doesn't carry itself seriously, and leaning into the imagination of the player to unravel the lore of the world while giving them a playground to explore in their own way. This game was more than just a prequel leading into the original, it was a reboot that redefined what Deus Ex is meant to be. And that destroyed the IP. Human Revolution sacrificed all the defining features of Deus Ex to create something new, something that fits into the same universe perhaps but leaves behind everything that made Deus Ex a truly excellent game.

If you want Deus Ex, this isn't it. But it is a great dystopian cyberpunk game nonetheless, and the only substantial negatives are that is fails to capture the legacy of Deus Ex.

The world in this game discusses transhumanism quite extensively, and frequently grapples with the ethics of transcendence and the definion of humanity throughout. The dystopian state of the environment is very tangible. This game tells a very personal story however of someone who is trapped in this world and recreated by it, rather than one which explores the broader topics. And while several of the characters have strong presence and distinct personality, they're seemingly designed with a particular moody factor that grounds them in unlikeability. 

This game is dark and pragmatic and holds back no punches in giving you a thorough cyberpunk simulation. A solid experience in its own right, and a game worth playing if you like this genre. It just isn't the Deus Ex that it was supposed to be, and ended up being another scar on the legacy of a very different and deeply tarnished universe that could have been better.
